name: Hardy-Weinberg: Homozygous Dominant Frequency (p^2)
description: Gives the expected frequency of homozygous dominant individuals in a Hardy-Weinberg population as the square of the dominant allele frequency p. The result is the proportion carrying two dominant alleles.
notes: Valid only under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (random mating, no selection, mutation, migration, or drift). Enter p as a decimal fraction between 0 and 1, not a percentage.

name: Hardy-Weinberg: Heterozygous Frequency (2pq)
description: Gives the expected frequency of heterozygous individuals in a Hardy-Weinberg population as 2 times the dominant allele frequency p times the recessive allele frequency q. The result is the proportion carrying one of each allele.
notes: Requires Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and p and q should sum to 1. Enter both as decimal fractions; heterozygote frequency is maximized when p equals q equals 0.5.

name: Hardy-Weinberg: Homozygous Recessive Frequency (q^2)
description: Gives the expected frequency of homozygous recessive individuals in a Hardy-Weinberg population as the square of the recessive allele frequency q. This is the proportion displaying the recessive phenotype.
notes: Only valid under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium; enter q as a decimal fraction. Because the recessive phenotype is directly observable, q squared is often the starting point for estimating allele frequencies.

name: Dominant Allele Frequency (p = 1 - q)
description: Calculates the dominant allele frequency p by subtracting the recessive allele frequency q from 1. It relies on the fact that the two allele frequencies at a biallelic locus must sum to 1.
notes: Applies to a locus with exactly two alleles; enter q as a decimal fraction between 0 and 1. The result is not meaningful if more than two alleles exist.

name: Allele Frequency from Genotype Counts
description: Estimates an allele's frequency directly from genotype counts, adding twice the homozygous count plus the heterozygous count and dividing by twice the total individuals. This counts the allele copies out of all alleles at the locus.
notes: Each individual carries two alleles, hence the factors of 2; homozygotes contribute two copies and heterozygotes one. This direct count needs no Hardy-Weinberg assumption.

name: Exponential Population Growth
description: Projects population size under unlimited exponential growth, multiplying the initial size by e raised to the growth rate times elapsed time. It models continuous growth with no resource limits.
notes: The growth rate and time units must match (both per the same time unit) since their product is a pure exponent. A negative rate models exponential decline; this ignores carrying capacity.

name: Logistic Population Growth Rate
description: Gives the instantaneous population growth rate under logistic dynamics, equal to the intrinsic rate times current size times the fraction of unused carrying capacity (K minus N over K). Growth slows to zero as the population approaches K.
notes: Population size and carrying capacity share the same unit; the result is individuals added per unit time, not a new population size. Growth is fastest near N equal to K over 2 and negative if N exceeds K.

name: Population Doubling Time
description: Calculates the time required for a population to double under exponential growth, dividing the natural log of 2 by the growth rate. It converts a continuous growth rate into a doubling interval.
notes: The result carries the inverse time unit of the growth rate, so a per-year rate gives years. It assumes constant exponential growth; the rate must be positive.

name: Doubling Time (Rule of 70)
description: Estimates doubling time by dividing 70 by the percentage growth rate. This rule-of-thumb approximates the exact natural-log formula for quantities growing at a steady percentage rate.
notes: The growth rate is entered as a percent number (for example 3.5, not 0.035). It is an approximation; the more exact constant is about 69.3, and accuracy drops at large rates.

name: Population Density
description: Calculates population density by dividing the number of individuals by the area they occupy. The result expresses how many individuals live per unit of area.
notes: Density is only as meaningful as the area chosen; the result unit here is individuals per hectare, matching the area input. Use a consistent area unit throughout.

name: Mark-Recapture (Lincoln-Petersen Index)
description: Estimates total population size from a mark-recapture study, multiplying the number marked in the first capture by the total caught in the second, then dividing by the number of marked animals recaptured. It scales up from the recapture ratio.
notes: Assumes a closed population, thorough mixing of marks, and no mark loss or effect on recapture. Small recapture numbers make the estimate unreliable, and the result rounds to whole individuals.

name: Per Capita Growth Rate
description: Calculates the per capita growth rate by subtracting deaths from births and dividing by population size. It expresses net population change per individual over the measurement period.
notes: Births, deaths, and population size cover the same time interval; the result is a rate per individual, not a total change. A positive value means net growth, negative means decline.

name: Population Growth Rate (Percent)
description: Computes the percentage change in a population by subtracting the initial from the final size, dividing by the initial size, and multiplying by 100. It shows the relative growth over the period.
notes: The result is a percentage relative to the initial population, which must be nonzero. A negative value indicates a population decline.

name: Michaelis-Menten Reaction Rate
description: Gives the initial reaction rate of an enzyme via the Michaelis-Menten equation: maximum rate times substrate concentration divided by the sum of the Michaelis constant and substrate concentration. Rate rises with substrate and saturates toward Vmax.
notes: Km and substrate concentration must share units so they add correctly; the result carries the same units as Vmax. When substrate equals Km, the rate is exactly half of Vmax.

name: Lineweaver-Burk (Reciprocal Rate 1/v)
description: Computes the reciprocal reaction rate 1/v used in the Lineweaver-Burk linearization of Michaelis-Menten kinetics, as 1/Vmax plus (Km/Vmax) times 1/substrate. Plotting this against 1/substrate yields a straight line for finding Km and Vmax.
notes: This double-reciprocal form magnifies errors at low substrate concentrations, so it is less reliable than nonlinear fitting. The result is in reciprocal rate units (min/µmol here).

name: Enzyme Catalytic Efficiency (kcat/Km)
description: Calculates an enzyme's catalytic efficiency by dividing the turnover number kcat by the Michaelis constant Km. This ratio measures how effectively an enzyme converts substrate at low substrate concentrations.
notes: Result units are per molar per second; higher values indicate a more efficient enzyme, with a diffusion limit around 10^8 to 10^9. Keep Km in molar to match the intended units.

name: Enzyme Turnover Number (kcat)
description: Determines the enzyme turnover number kcat by dividing the maximum reaction rate Vmax by the total enzyme concentration. It represents how many substrate molecules one active site converts per second at saturation.
notes: Vmax and enzyme concentration must be in matching molar-based units so the result comes out per second. This assumes each enzyme molecule has one active site.

name: Q10 Temperature Coefficient
description: Calculates the Q10 temperature coefficient, the factor by which a reaction or biological rate changes per 10 degree rise in temperature, from the ratio of two rates raised to 10 divided by the temperature difference. It quantifies temperature sensitivity.
notes: The two rates use the same units so their ratio is dimensionless; a Q10 near 2 to 3 is typical for biological processes. Temperatures must be entered so t2 exceeds t1.

name: Metabolic Rate (Kleiber's Law)
description: Estimates an animal's basal metabolic rate from Kleiber's law, as 70 times body mass raised to the power 0.75. It captures the allometric scaling where metabolism rises less than proportionally with body mass.
notes: Body mass is in kilograms and the result is approximately kcal per day; the 3/4-power exponent is an empirical scaling law across species. Constants vary somewhat between sources.

name: Net Primary Productivity
description: Calculates net primary productivity as gross primary productivity minus respiration loss. It represents the energy or biomass that primary producers make available to the rest of the ecosystem after their own metabolic costs.
notes: Both inputs must share the same rate unit (mass per area per time here); the result carries that unit. A negative value means respiration exceeds production over the period.

name: Standing Biomass
description: Calculates standing biomass by multiplying the number of individuals by the mean mass per individual. It gives the total mass of living organisms present at one point in time.
notes: The result unit matches the per-individual mass unit (grams here). This is a snapshot of biomass present, not a production rate over time.

name: Shannon Diversity Index (Two Species)
description: Calculates the Shannon diversity index for a two-species community, as the negative sum of each species' proportion times the natural log of that proportion. Higher values reflect greater diversity and evenness.
notes: Proportions must be decimal fractions that sum to 1, and each must be greater than zero (ln of zero is undefined). Using natural log gives the index in nats; add terms for more species.

name: Simpson's Dominance Index (D)
description: Calculates Simpson's dominance index for a two-species community, summing the square of each species' proportion. It gives the probability that two randomly drawn individuals belong to the same species, rising as one species dominates.
notes: Proportions must be decimal fractions summing to 1. Higher D means lower diversity; it is the complement of Simpson's diversity index (1 minus D).

name: Simpson's Diversity Index (1 - D)
description: Calculates Simpson's diversity index for a two-species community as 1 minus the sum of squared proportions. It gives the probability that two randomly drawn individuals belong to different species, rising with greater diversity.
notes: Proportions must be decimal fractions summing to 1; for two species the result ranges from 0 to 0.5 (reached when both are equally common). Higher values mean greater diversity, the opposite of the dominance index D.

name: Sørensen Similarity Coefficient
description: Calculates the Sørensen similarity coefficient between two sites, as twice the number of shared species divided by the total species counts of both sites. It measures how similar two communities are in species composition.
notes: The result ranges from 0 (no shared species) to 1 (identical species lists); it uses presence-absence data, not abundances. Shared species are counted once but weighted double in the numerator.

name: Microscope Total Magnification
description: Calculates the total magnification of a compound microscope by multiplying the objective lens magnification by the eyepiece magnification. The result shows how many times larger the specimen appears than its actual size.
notes: Both inputs are dimensionless magnification factors, and the result is likewise a times-factor. Total magnification does not indicate resolution, which depends on numerical aperture.

name: Surface-Area-to-Volume Ratio (Sphere)
description: Gives the surface-area-to-volume ratio of a sphere, which equals 3/r since surface area is 4pi*r squared and volume is (4/3)pi*r cubed. Smaller radii yield larger ratios, reflecting how tiny cells exchange material more efficiently.
notes: The ratio has units of inverse length, so it depends on the length unit used for the radius. Valid only for a perfect sphere; irregular shapes have higher ratios for the same volume.

name: Nernst Equilibrium Potential (Monovalent, 37°C)
description: Computes the equilibrium (reversal) membrane potential for a monovalent cation at body temperature using the Nernst equation, from the ratio of extracellular to intracellular concentration. The result is the voltage at which diffusion and electrical forces on the ion balance.
notes: The 61.5 mV factor assumes 37 degrees C and a valence of +1; use a negative sign for anions like chloride. Only the concentration ratio matters, so both must share the same units.

name: Bacterial Generation Time
description: Determines the doubling (generation) time of a bacterial culture in exponential growth, dividing the elapsed time by the number of doublings, which is the base-2 logarithm of the final-to-initial cell count ratio. It is the average time for the population to double.
notes: Assumes exponential (log-phase) growth with no lag or death. The final count must exceed the initial count so the number of doublings is positive; time and generation time share the same unit.

name: Fick's Law of Diffusion (Flux)
description: Calculates the rate of diffusion of a substance across a membrane by Fick's law, as the diffusion coefficient times the area times the concentration difference, divided by the membrane thickness. A steeper gradient, larger area, or thinner membrane speeds transport.
notes: Assumes steady-state passive diffusion down a linear concentration gradient. Keep units consistent; mismatched concentration and length units will make the resulting flux units meaningless.

name: Water Potential (Osmosis)
description: Computes total water potential as the sum of solute potential and pressure potential, psi = psi_s + psi_p. Water potential predicts the direction of osmotic water movement across plant cell membranes.
notes: Solute potential is normally negative or zero, and pressure (turgor) potential is normally positive or zero. Water moves from higher to lower (more negative) total water potential.

name: Cell Count After N Divisions
description: Gives the number of cells produced from one starting cell after n rounds of mitotic division, 2^n. Each division doubles the cell population.
notes: Assumes every cell divides synchronously with no cell death. n is typically a non-negative integer; n=0 gives the single starting cell.

name: Nerve Impulse Conduction Velocity (Two-Point Stimulation)
description: Calculates the conduction velocity of a nerve impulse using the two-point (near/far) stimulation method, in which the same nerve is stimulated at two points a known distance apart and the difference in response latency is measured. The velocity equals the distance between the two stimulation points divided by the difference in response times.
notes: Assumes conduction velocity is constant along the segment between the two stimulation points and that both electrodes stimulate the same nerve fiber population; typical results range from about 0.5 to 120 m/s depending on fiber type and myelination.

name: Renal Tubular Reabsorption Rate (%)
description: Calculates the percentage of a filtered substance that is reabsorbed by the renal tubules, based on the clearance of that substance relative to the glomerular filtration rate (GFR, typically measured via inulin clearance). A high reabsorption rate indicates the substance is largely retained by the body rather than excreted.
notes: Assumes GFR is measured accurately (e.g., via inulin clearance) and that urine and plasma concentrations are measured simultaneously at steady state; a negative result would indicate net tubular secretion rather than reabsorption.

name: Weber's Law (Weber Fraction)
description: Calculates the Weber fraction, the ratio of the just-noticeable difference (JND) in a stimulus to the baseline stimulus intensity. According to Weber's law, this ratio is approximately constant across a wide range of baseline intensities for a given sensory modality.
notes: The Weber fraction is only approximately constant within a mid-range of stimulus intensities; it tends to break down at very low or very high intensities near the absolute threshold or saturation.

name: Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz Equation (Resting Membrane Potential)
description: Calculates the resting membrane potential of a cell using the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz (GHK) equation, which accounts for the relative membrane permeabilities and the intracellular/extracellular concentrations of K+, Na+, and Cl-. Unlike the simpler Nernst equation, it produces a single steady-state potential reflecting the combined contributions of all three ions.
notes: The coefficient 61.5 (≈ 2.303·RT/F) assumes a temperature of about 37°C (mammalian body temperature); for experiments at room temperature (~20°C), the standard coefficient is closer to 58 and would need to be adjusted accordingly.

name: Expected Heterozygosity (Biallelic)
description: Computes expected heterozygosity at a biallelic locus under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium as 1 minus the sum of squared allele frequencies. It is the probability that two randomly drawn alleles differ, a measure of genetic diversity.
notes: Allele frequencies p and q are proportions that should sum to 1; the result is between 0 and 0.5 for two alleles. It assumes Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and no more than two alleles.

name: Effective Number of Alleles (Biallelic)
description: Computes the effective number of alleles as the reciprocal of the sum of squared allele frequencies. It is the number of equally frequent alleles that would give the same homozygosity, indicating evenness of allele frequencies.
notes: Allele frequencies should sum to 1; the result ranges from 1 (fixed) up to 2 for a biallelic locus. It is highest when the two alleles are equally frequent.

name: Fixation Index (Fst)
description: Computes Wright's fixation index Fst as (Ht - Hs)/Ht, the reduction in heterozygosity due to population subdivision. It measures genetic differentiation among subpopulations relative to the total.
notes: Ht and Hs are heterozygosities between 0 and 1 with Ht at least Hs; the result is between 0 and 1. Values near 0 indicate little differentiation, near 1 near-complete separation.

name: Inbreeding Coefficient (F = 1 - Ho/He)
description: Computes the inbreeding coefficient F as 1 minus the ratio of observed to expected heterozygosity. It quantifies the deficit of heterozygotes relative to Hardy-Weinberg expectation, reflecting inbreeding or population structure.
notes: Ho and He are heterozygosities between 0 and 1. Positive F indicates a heterozygote deficit (inbreeding); negative F an excess (e.g. outbreeding), so results can fall below zero.

name: Inbreeding Coefficient (Wright's Path)
description: Computes the inbreeding coefficient contributed by one ancestral loop in a pedigree via Wright's path method, as (1/2)^L times (1 + Fa), where L is the number of individuals on the path linking the two parents through the common ancestor. It quantifies expected homozygosity from a shared ancestor.
notes: L counts the individuals on the path from one parent through the common ancestor to the other parent (both parents included); Fa is that ancestor's own inbreeding, 0 if non-inbred. Multiple independent loops must be summed separately.

name: Haldane Mapping Function
description: Converts genetic map distance to recombination frequency using Haldane's function, 0.5(1 - exp(-2d)), which assumes no crossover interference. It gives the expected fraction of recombinant gametes for a given map distance.
notes: Map distance d is in Morgans (1 Morgan = 100 cM), not centimorgans; the result approaches 0.5 as distance grows. It ignores interference, so it slightly misfits closely spaced loci where interference matters.

name: Haldane Map Distance (from Recombination)
description: Inverts Haldane's mapping function to obtain map distance from recombination frequency, as -0.5·ln(1 - 2·rf). It corrects the raw recombination fraction for unobserved multiple crossovers to give an additive distance.
notes: Recombination frequency rf is a proportion below 0.5; the result is in Morgans. As rf approaches 0.5 the distance diverges to infinity, and values at or above 0.5 are undefined.

name: Kosambi Map Distance
description: Converts recombination frequency to map distance using Kosambi's function, 0.25·ln((1+2rf)/(1-2rf)), which allows for crossover interference that decreases with distance. It often fits real genetic data better than Haldane's over short intervals.
notes: Recombination frequency rf is a proportion below 0.5; the result is in Morgans. It diverges as rf nears 0.5 and is undefined at or above it; interference is modeled, not measured.

name: Broad-Sense Heritability
description: Computes broad-sense heritability as the ratio of total genetic variance to phenotypic variance. It is the fraction of trait variation in a population attributable to all genetic effects, including dominance and epistasis.
notes: Both variances are on the same squared-trait scale; the result is a proportion between 0 and 1. It is population- and environment-specific and does not predict response to selection, unlike narrow-sense heritability.

name: Narrow-Sense Heritability
description: Computes narrow-sense heritability as the ratio of additive genetic variance to phenotypic variance. It is the fraction of trait variation passed on predictably from parents to offspring, and it governs response to selection.
notes: Both variances share the same squared-trait scale; the result is between 0 and 1. Only additive variance is counted, so it is always at most the broad-sense heritability.

name: Breeder's Equation (Response to Selection)
description: Predicts the response to selection as the product of narrow-sense heritability and the selection differential. It estimates how much a trait's mean will shift in the next generation given the selection applied to parents.
notes: Heritability is a proportion between 0 and 1; the response takes the same units as the selection differential. It assumes constant heritability and no environmental change, so it holds best for one generation.

name: Realized Heritability
description: Computes realized heritability as the observed response to selection divided by the selection differential. It estimates narrow-sense heritability retrospectively from the actual outcome of a selection experiment.
notes: Response and selection differential must be in the same trait units so the ratio is dimensionless between 0 and 1. It is an empirical estimate over one or more generations and can be biased by drift or environmental shifts.

name: Selection Coefficient
description: Computes the selection coefficient as one minus the relative fitness of a genotype. It measures the proportional reduction in fitness of that genotype compared with the fittest reference genotype.
notes: Relative fitness is scaled so the fittest genotype equals 1; the result lies between 0 (no selection) and 1 (lethal). A fitness above 1 would give a negative coefficient, indicating favored selection.

name: Allele Frequency Change (Selection Against Recessive)
description: Computes the per-generation change in a recessive allele's frequency under selection against the recessive homozygote, as -s·q^2(1-q)/(1-s·q^2). The negative value shows how quickly selection removes the deleterious allele.
notes: Selection coefficient s and allele frequency q are proportions between 0 and 1. Change slows sharply as q gets small because rare recessives are hidden in heterozygotes, so elimination is never complete.

name: Mutation-Selection Balance (Recessive)
description: Computes the equilibrium frequency of a recessive deleterious allele under mutation-selection balance as the square root of the mutation rate divided by the selection coefficient. It is the frequency where new mutations balance selective removal.
notes: Mutation rate mu and selection coefficient s are dimensionless per-generation values; the result is an allele frequency between 0 and 1. It assumes a fully recessive allele; even slight dominance greatly lowers the equilibrium.

name: Mutation-Selection Balance (Dominant)
description: Estimates the equilibrium frequency of a deleterious dominant (or partially dominant) allele where new mutations are balanced by selection removing them. The frequency equals the mutation rate mu divided by the product of the dominance coefficient h and selection coefficient s.
notes: Valid when h*s is not too small (partial or full dominance); for fully recessive alleles (h=0) use the recessive form sqrt(mu/s) instead. All coefficients are dimensionless fractions.

name: Effective Population Size (Sex Ratio)
description: Computes the effective population size when the numbers of breeding males and females differ, using the harmonic-like formula 4*Nm*Nf/(Nm+Nf). A skewed sex ratio lowers Ne below the census count, increasing genetic drift.
notes: Only breeding individuals are counted, not the total census size. When Nm equals Nf the result equals the total number of breeders; extreme skew drives Ne toward four times the rarer sex.

name: Effective Population Size (Harmonic Mean, 2 Gens)
description: Gives the long-term effective population size across two generations as the harmonic mean of the two generation sizes, 2/(1/N1+1/N2). It captures how a temporary bottleneck disproportionately reduces effective size.
notes: The harmonic mean is dominated by the smallest value, so a single small generation lowers Ne far more than a large one raises it. Extend the denominator with more terms for additional generations.

name: Heterozygosity Decay (Genetic Drift)
description: Predicts the expected heterozygosity remaining after t generations of drift in a population of effective size Ne, since each generation retains a fraction 1-1/(2*Ne) of the previous heterozygosity. Smaller Ne means faster loss of genetic variation.
notes: Assumes an ideal Wright-Fisher population with no mutation, selection, or migration. Ne is the effective, not census, size; t is measured in generations, and H0 lies between 0 and 1.

name: Nei's Genetic Distance
description: Converts Nei's genetic identity I between two populations into a genetic distance by taking the negative natural logarithm, -ln(I). Larger distances indicate populations that share fewer alleles at similar frequencies.
notes: Identity I must lie between 0 and 1; I=1 gives distance 0 (identical), and small I yields large distances. The measure assumes drift and mutation but no strong selection.

name: Allele Frequency Under Migration
description: Projects an allele frequency after t generations of one-way migration toward a source with allele frequency qm. Starting from q0, the deviation q0-qm shrinks by a factor (1-m) each generation, so the frequency converges toward qm.
notes: Migration rate m is the fraction of the population replaced by migrants per generation and must lie between 0 and 1. The migrant frequency qm is treated as constant; larger m means faster convergence.

name: Mutation Equilibrium Allele Frequency
description: Gives the equilibrium frequency of an allele when forward mutation (rate mu) and backward mutation (rate nu) balance, equal to mu/(mu+nu). The allele favored by the higher mutation rate predominates at equilibrium.
notes: This mutation-only equilibrium ignores selection and drift and is reached very slowly because mutation rates are tiny. Both rates are per-generation probabilities; the result depends only on their ratio.

name: Allele Frequency After Mutation (One-Way)
description: Tracks how an allele frequency declines under recurrent one-way mutation over t generations. Each generation multiplies the frequency by (1-mu), so starting at q0 it decays geometrically toward zero.
notes: Selection, drift, and back-mutation are ignored, and mu is a per-generation probability between 0 and 1. Because mutation rates are small, appreciable change requires many generations.

name: Wahlund Effect (Heterozygote Deficit)
description: Quantifies the reduction in heterozygote frequency caused by population subdivision (the Wahlund effect). The deficit equals 2*p*q*Fst, the expected heterozygosity times the fixation index Fst measuring differentiation among subpopulations.
notes: Fst ranges from 0 (no subdivision, no deficit) to 1 (complete differentiation); p and q are allele frequencies that should sum to 1. The result is how much observed heterozygosity falls below Hardy-Weinberg expectation.

name: Linkage Disequilibrium Coefficient (D)
description: Measures linkage disequilibrium between two loci as D = x11 - p1*q1, the difference between the observed AB haplotype frequency and the product expected under independence. Nonzero D means alleles A and B are statistically associated.
notes: D can be positive or negative and its range depends on the allele frequencies, making it hard to compare across loci; use r-squared or D-prime for standardized comparisons. All frequencies must be consistent (0 to 1).

name: Linkage Disequilibrium (r-squared)
description: Computes the standardized linkage disequilibrium r-squared from the coefficient D and the four allele frequencies, as D^2 divided by p1*(1-p1)*q1*(1-q1). It ranges from 0 (independence) to 1 (complete association) and is comparable across loci.
notes: p1 and q1 are the frequencies of alleles A and B; the denominator uses their complements, so neither allele frequency may be 0 or 1. r-squared relates directly to the correlation between the two loci.

name: Mean Population Fitness (One Locus)
description: Calculates the mean fitness of a population for a single biallelic locus by weighting each genotype's fitness by its Hardy-Weinberg frequency: p^2*w11 + 2*p*q*w12 + q^2*w22. This average determines the direction of allele-frequency change.
notes: Allele frequencies p and q should sum to 1, and the fitness values are relative (often scaled so the best genotype equals 1). Assumes Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions before selection.

name: Balanced Polymorphism (Overdominance Equilibrium)
description: Gives the stable equilibrium frequency of allele a under overdominance (heterozygote advantage), where both homozygotes are selected against. The equilibrium q equals s1/(s1+s2), with s1 the selection coefficient against AA and s2 that against aa.
notes: Requires genuine heterozygote advantage (both s1 and s2 positive) for a stable polymorphism; the equilibrium is independent of initial frequencies. Selection coefficients are dimensionless fractions between 0 and 1.

name: Nei's Genetic Identity
description: Computes Nei's normalized genetic identity between populations X and Y as Jxy/sqrt(Jx*Jy), where Jxy is the cross-population probability of identical alleles and Jx, Jy the within-population values. It ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 meaning identical allele frequencies.
notes: The J values are sums of allele-frequency products across loci, so Jx and Jy must be positive. Identity is the quantity whose negative log gives Nei's genetic distance.

name: Wright's F-statistics (Fit)
description: Combines the within-subpopulation inbreeding Fis and the among-subpopulation differentiation Fst into the overall inbreeding coefficient Fit = Fis + Fst - Fis*Fst. Fit measures the total reduction in heterozygosity of an individual relative to the total population.
notes: The relationship comes from (1-Fit) = (1-Fis)(1-Fst); Fst ranges from 0 to 1, while Fis can be negative under heterozygote excess, which then lowers Fit.

name: Genotype Frequency Under Inbreeding (AA)
description: Gives the frequency of the homozygous AA genotype in an inbred population as p^2 + F*p*q, where F is the inbreeding coefficient. Inbreeding adds F*p*q to the random-mating expectation p^2, increasing homozygote frequency.
notes: Allele frequencies p and q should sum to 1 and F ranges from 0 (random mating) to 1 (complete inbreeding). The matching heterozygote frequency is reduced to 2*p*q*(1-F).

name: Additive Genetic Variance (Biallelic)
description: Computes the additive genetic variance contributed by a single biallelic locus as 2*p*q*alpha^2, where alpha is the average effect of an allele substitution. This variance is the component of phenotypic variation that responds to selection.
notes: Allele frequencies p and q should sum to 1; variance is maximized at intermediate frequencies and vanishes as either allele nears fixation. alpha is in trait units, so the variance is in squared trait units.

name: Coefficient of Relationship (Path Counting)
description: Computes the coefficient of relationship between two relatives as 0.5 raised to the number of meioses (generational links) separating them along a single path, e.g. n=1 for parent-child, n=2 for full siblings or grandparent-grandchild.
notes: Each meiosis halves the expected fraction of shared alleles inherited by descent. For relatives connected by multiple paths (e.g. full siblings), sum the coefficient over each separate path.

name: Recombination Frequency (from Offspring Counts)
description: Estimates the recombination frequency between two linked genes from a test-cross or F2 offspring count, expressed as the percentage of recombinant offspring among the total. This value is used to construct genetic linkage maps, where 1% recombination frequency corresponds to 1 map unit (centimorgan).
notes: Valid only when the two genes are linked on the same chromosome (a recombination frequency of 50% indicates independent assortment or genes far apart); assumes offspring counts are large enough to be statistically reliable.

name: Molecular Clock: Divergence Time

variables.label: Substitution rate per site per year

description: Estimates the time since two lineages diverged from a common ancestor using the molecular clock hypothesis. It divides the observed proportion of sequence differences between the two lineages by twice the substitution rate, since substitutions accumulate independently along both branches since divergence.
notes: Assumes a constant (clock-like) substitution rate over time and that the two lineages are not under differing selective pressures; results can be highly sensitive to the assumed substitution rate.

name: Molecular Clock: Substitution Rate
description: Calculates the per-site, per-year nucleotide substitution rate from a known divergence time and the observed proportion of sequence difference between two lineages, typically calibrated using fossil or geological dating of the divergence event.
notes: Assumes a constant substitution rate (molecular clock) between the two lineages and requires an independently calibrated divergence time; results are typically extremely small numbers (on the order of 1e-8 to 1e-9 per site per year).

name: Twin Study Heritability (Falconer's Formula)
description: Estimates the broad-sense heritability (H²) of a trait using Falconer's formula, which doubles the difference in concordance rates between monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twins. Because MZ twins share ~100% of their genes and DZ twins share ~50% on average, doubling the gap isolates the genetic contribution to trait variance.
notes: Assumes equal environmental similarity between MZ and DZ twin pairs (the 'equal environments assumption') and no gene-environment interaction; results are theoretically bounded between 0 and 1, but sampling error can occasionally produce values outside this range.

name: ABO Blood Type: Type A Phenotype Frequency
description: Calculates the expected population frequency of the type A blood phenotype under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the ABO locus, which has three alleles (IA, IB, i) with frequencies p, q, and r respectively (p+q+r=1). Type A individuals arise from either the IAIA homozygous genotype (p²) or the IAi heterozygous genotype (2pr), since the i allele is recessive to IA.
notes: Assumes the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (random mating, no selection, mutation, migration, or drift) and that p, q, r are consistent with p+q+r=1; the unused allele frequency q (for IB) is implicitly 1-p-r.

name: ABO Blood Type: O Allele Frequency (from Phenotype)

variables.label: Frequency of O blood type phenotype

description: Derives the frequency of the recessive O allele (i) from the observed frequency of the O blood type phenotype, under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Since the O phenotype arises only from the homozygous ii genotype (frequency r²), the allele frequency r is obtained by taking the square root of the phenotype frequency.
notes: Assumes Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and that the O phenotype frequency was measured accurately from a representative population sample; the resulting r can then be used with the ABO type A/B formulas.

name: PCR Product Copies after n Cycles
description: Gives the number of DNA copies after n PCR cycles at a given efficiency (1 = perfect doubling).
notes: Real reactions plateau as reagents run out.

name: qPCR Efficiency from Standard-Curve Slope

variables.label: Slope of Ct vs log₁₀ quantity

description: Gives amplification efficiency from the slope of a qPCR standard curve; −3.32 means 100 %.
notes: Acceptable assays are usually 90–110 %.

name: Relative Expression (ΔΔCt Method)
description: Gives the fold change in gene expression relative to a control, normalised to a reference gene (Livak and Schmittgen 2001).
notes: Assumes about 100 % efficiency for both genes.

name: DNA Concentration from A260
description: Gives double-stranded DNA concentration from UV absorbance: one A260 unit ≈ 50 µg/mL (40 for RNA, 33 for single-stranded DNA).
notes: A260/A280 near 1.8 indicates pure DNA.

name: DNA Copy Number from Mass
description: Converts a mass of double-stranded DNA into the number of molecules (650 g/mol per base pair).
notes: Used to prepare qPCR standards.

name: Molar Amount of DNA from Mass
description: Converts micrograms of double-stranded DNA into picomoles, as needed for ligations and sequencing.
notes: 1 µg of a 3 kb plasmid ≈ 0.51 pmol.

name: Ligation Insert Mass for a Molar Ratio
description: Gives how much insert DNA to add to a ligation for a chosen molar ratio to the vector (commonly 3:1).
notes: Short inserts need higher ratios.

name: Primer Melting Temperature (Wallace Rule)
description: Estimates the melting temperature of a short oligonucleotide (under about 14–20 bases).
notes: Use a nearest-neighbour calculator for longer primers.

name: Primer Melting Temperature (Salt-Adjusted)
description: Estimates oligonucleotide melting temperature allowing for salt concentration and length.
notes: Primer pairs should be within about 5 °C of each other.

name: GC Content
description: Gives the share of G and C bases in a DNA sequence, which affects stability and PCR design.
notes: Primers usually aim for 40–60 %.

name: Centrifuge Relative Centrifugal Force from rpm
description: Converts rotor speed into relative centrifugal force (g-force) so protocols transfer between centrifuges.
notes: Protocols should state × g, not rpm.

name: Centrifuge rpm for a Required g-Force
description: Gives the rotor speed that produces a required g-force.
notes: Use the radius to the bottom of the tube for the maximum RCF.

name: Haemocytometer Cell Count
description: Gives cell concentration from a haemocytometer count: each large square holds 0.1 µL.
notes: Count 100–300 cells for good precision.

name: Population Doublings of a Cell Culture
description: Gives the number of population doublings between seeding and harvest, used to track cell-line age.
notes: Primary cells stop dividing after a limited number (Hayflick limit).

name: Transformation Efficiency
description: Gives the number of transformants per microgram of plasmid DNA.
notes: Good chemically competent cells give 10⁶–10⁹ cfu/µg.

name: Fraction of Cells Infected at an MOI (Poisson)
description: Gives the share of cells receiving at least one virus particle when virus is added at a multiplicity of infection, assuming random (Poisson) distribution.
notes: MOI 3 infects about 95 %.

name: Virus Titre from Plaque Count
description: Gives the concentration of infectious virus from a plaque assay.
notes: Count plates with about 30–300 plaques.

name: Protein Molecular Weight from Length
description: Estimates a protein's molecular weight from its length using an average of 110 Da per residue.
notes: Actual weight depends on composition and modifications.

name: Protein Concentration from A280
description: Gives protein concentration from UV absorbance with the protein's extinction coefficient (from its Trp and Tyr content).

name: FRET Efficiency from Distance
description: Gives the energy transfer efficiency between two fluorophores; it falls steeply with distance, making FRET a molecular ruler.
notes: Exactly 50 % at the Förster radius.

name: Enzyme Specific Activity
description: Gives enzyme units per milligram of protein, which rises as an enzyme is purified.
notes: Fold purification = final ÷ initial specific activity.

name: Bacterial OD600 to Cell Density
description: Estimates E. coli cell density from optical density at 600 nm (OD 1 ≈ 8 × 10⁸ cells/mL).
notes: Calibrate for your strain and spectrophotometer.

name: Cell Seeding Volume
description: Gives the volume of cell suspension needed to seed a set of wells at a target number per well.
notes: Prepare about 10 % extra.

name: Sedimentation Coefficient (Svedberg Equation)
description: Gives the sedimentation coefficient in svedbergs from molar mass, buoyancy and friction (Svedberg).
notes: Ribosomes 70S/80S are named from this.

name: Stokes–Einstein Diffusion Coefficient
description: Gives the diffusion coefficient of a spherical particle or protein in a fluid.
notes: Dynamic light scattering uses it in reverse to size particles.

name: Resting Heart Rate from Body Mass (Allometry)
description: Estimates a mammal's resting heart rate from body mass (allometric scaling).
notes: A mouse beats about 600 times a minute, an elephant about 30.

name: Law of Laplace (Vessel Wall Stress)
description: Gives the wall stress of a spherical chamber (heart, alveolus, aneurysm); use p·r/h for a cylindrical vessel.
notes: Why dilated hearts and large aneurysms are under more stress.

name: Starling Filtration across a Capillary
description: Gives net fluid movement out of a capillary from hydrostatic and oncotic pressures (Starling 1896).
notes: Positive = filtration into tissue; negative = reabsorption.

name: Oxygen Saturation from PO₂ (Severinghaus)
description: Estimates haemoglobin oxygen saturation from oxygen partial pressure (Severinghaus 1979).
notes: PO₂ 60 mmHg ≈ 90 % — the steep part of the curve starts below.

name: Neuron Length Constant
description: Gives the distance over which a voltage change decays to 37 % along a passive axon or dendrite (cable theory).
notes: Myelin raises r_m, extending the length constant.

name: Membrane Time Constant
description: Gives how fast a neuron's membrane voltage responds to current: τ = R_m·C_m.
notes: Typical neurons are 10–30 ms.

name: Glomerular Filtration from Starling Forces
description: Gives the glomerular filtration rate from the net filtration pressure across the glomerulus.
notes: Normal net pressure is about 10 mmHg.

name: Oxygen Extraction Fraction
description: Gives the share of delivered oxygen that tissues take up; normal is about 25 %, higher in shock or heart failure.
notes: Rises when oxygen delivery falls.

name: Metabolic Equivalent from VO₂
description: Converts oxygen uptake into METs, multiples of resting metabolism (1 MET = 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min).
notes: Brisk walking is about 3–4 METs; running 10 km/h about 10.

name: Energy Expenditure from Oxygen Uptake
description: Estimates energy used from oxygen consumed at about 5 kcal per litre of oxygen.
notes: The exact figure depends on the fuel mix (4.7–5.05 kcal/L).

name: LOD Score for Linkage
expression: rc * log(th) + nr * log(1 - th) - (rc + nr) * log(0.5)
description: Gives the log-odds that two loci are linked at recombination fraction θ versus unlinked (Morton 1955).
notes: A LOD of 3 or more is conventional evidence of linkage.

name: Mutation Rate from a Fluctuation Test (p₀ Method)

variables.label: Fraction of cultures with no mutants

description: Estimates the mutation rate from the share of parallel cultures with no mutants (Luria and Delbrück 1943).
notes: Works best when 10–70 % of cultures have no mutants.

name: Expected Coalescence Time of Two Gene Copies
description: Gives the expected time back to the common ancestor of two gene copies in a diploid population (Kingman's coalescent: 2Nₑ generations).
notes: For a whole sample it tends to 4Nₑ generations.

name: Probability of a Genotype from Parents (Two Heterozygotes)
description: Gives the chance that exactly k of n children of two carrier parents have a recessive condition (probability ¼ each).
notes: Each birth is independent.

name: Heritability from Parent–Offspring Regression

variables.label: Slope of offspring on one parent

description: Gives narrow-sense heritability from the regression of offspring values on one parent; use the slope directly for the mid-parent.
notes: Assumes no shared-environment effects.

name: Log Reduction of Microbes
description: Gives the number of ten-fold reductions achieved by disinfection or sterilisation.
notes: 4-log = 99.99 % killed.

name: Percent Killed from Log Reduction
description: Converts a log reduction into the percentage of microbes killed.

name: Thermal Resistance z-Value
description: Gives the temperature rise that cuts a microbe's D-value ten-fold.
notes: About 10 °C for bacterial spores.

name: Monod Specific Growth Rate
description: Gives a microbial culture's growth rate as a function of limiting nutrient (Monod 1949).
notes: Same shape as Michaelis–Menten kinetics.

name: Chemostat Steady-State Substrate
description: Gives the limiting-nutrient concentration in a chemostat at steady state, where growth rate equals dilution rate.
notes: Wash-out occurs if D approaches μmax.

name: Biomass Yield Coefficient
description: Gives grams of cells produced per gram of substrate consumed.
notes: E. coli on glucose is about 0.5 g/g aerobically.

name: Colony Count per mL (Plate Count)
description: Gives viable microbes per mL of the original sample from a plate count.
notes: Count plates with 30–300 colonies.

name: Fechner's Law (Perceived Intensity)
description: Gives perceived sensation as proportional to the logarithm of stimulus intensity (Fechner 1860).
notes: Stevens' power law often fits better.

name: Stevens' Power Law
description: Gives perceived magnitude as a power of stimulus intensity; the exponent depends on the sense (Stevens 1957).
notes: Exponents below 1 compress, above 1 expand.

name: Visual Acuity: Snellen to logMAR
description: Converts a Snellen fraction such as 6/12 or 20/40 into logMAR, the scale used in research.

name: Decimal Visual Acuity from logMAR
description: Converts logMAR into decimal visual acuity (1.0 = normal).
notes: 0.3 logMAR ≈ 0.5 decimal.

name: Pure-Tone Average Hearing Level
description: Averages hearing thresholds at the main speech frequencies to grade hearing loss (WHO uses 500–4000 Hz).
notes: WHO: below 20 normal, 20–34 mild, 35–49 moderate.

name: Hardy–Weinberg Chi-Square Test (Two Alleles)
description: Tests whether genotype counts fit Hardy–Weinberg proportions; compare with χ² on 1 degree of freedom.
notes: Departures can signal selection, inbreeding or genotyping errors.

name: Fixation Probability of a Beneficial Mutation (Haldane)
description: Gives the chance that a new mutation with small advantage s eventually spreads through a large population (Haldane 1927).
notes: Even beneficial mutations are usually lost by chance.

name: Fixation Probability of a Neutral Mutation
description: Gives the chance a single new neutral mutation in a diploid population drifts to fixation.
notes: So the neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate (Kimura).

name: Respiratory Exchange and Fat Oxidation Rate
description: Estimates fat burned from oxygen uptake and CO₂ output during exercise (Péronnet and Massicotte 1991).
notes: Carbohydrate oxidation is 4.585 V̇CO₂ − 3.226 V̇O₂.

name: Carbohydrate Oxidation Rate
description: Estimates carbohydrate burned from gas exchange during steady exercise (Péronnet and Massicotte 1991).
notes: Rises steeply with intensity.

name: Competitive Inhibition Rate
description: Gives the enzyme rate with a competitive inhibitor, which raises the apparent K_m by (1 + [I]/K_i) but leaves V_max unchanged.
notes: Enough substrate can outcompete the inhibitor.

name: Hill Equation (Cooperative Binding)
description: Gives the fraction of binding sites occupied when binding is cooperative (Hill 1910); n > 1 gives the S-shaped curve of haemoglobin.
notes: Haemoglobin has n ≈ 2.8.
